questions.stem: According to the author's own definition, what is data?
options: The features and activities of an object
Any number stored in a computer
Information that has already been analysed
questions.explanation: The chapter's key phrase is "Features and Activities of an Object is Data": the descriptive features of an object and the actions associated with it.

questions.stem: The word "data" comes from the Latin "datum". What does datum mean?
questions.explanation: Datum means "something given" — a foundational input, a starting point; the French "données" carries the same root.

questions.stem: In the data world, what is an "object" called?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that in the data world an object is called an entity, its features are attributes, and its activities are transactions.

questions.stem: In the car example in I Am Datapedia!, which of these is an INTERNAL activity of the car?
options: The car being sold to a new owner
An insurance policy affecting its value
Its mileage decreasing over time through engine wear
A modification made by the owner
The car being leased to a company
questions.explanation: Internal activities are changes that occur within the object itself, driven by its own properties and conditions; buying, selling, leasing and modifications are external.

questions.stem: What must corporate data be tied to in order to be valuable?
options: Return on Investment (ROI) of at least one line of business
The number of employees who use it
questions.explanation: "For Corporate, 'Data MUST tag with ROI'" — each line of business has data and an ROI model, and data should align with those business goals.

questions.stem: What criticism does I Am Datapedia! make of the traditional DIKW (data–information–knowledge–wisdom) model?
options: It does not capture the continuous, iterative nature of the data cycle
It applies only to machine learning
questions.explanation: Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom is helpful but linear; in reality one cycle's output becomes another's input, perpetually.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the three states of data?
options: All of these are named states
questions.explanation: The three states are data-at-rest, data-in-transit and data-in-use; "data-in-archive" is not one of them.

options: Data about data, which offers context and improves accessibility
Core entities such as customers or products
Records of user actions and habits
Data that is currently being transferred
questions.explanation: Metadata is data about data; master and reference data are the core entities; transactional data captures actions and habits.

questions.stem: How does data differ from traditional assets such as machinery?
options: Data must be replaced every year
Data gains value through use instead of being depleted
Data cannot be owned by an organisation
Data has a fixed expiry date
questions.explanation: Physical assets deplete or depreciate with use; data's utility increases with each use, it generates more data, and it has no expiry date.

questions.stem: Among data's unique properties, what does every interaction with data produce?
options: Metadata such as who accessed it, when and why
questions.explanation: "Generates more data": every interaction produces metadata — who accessed it, when and for what purpose — which is itself useful data.
